Ficus carica.npk: Balanced 8-8-8 or 10-10-10; switch to lower nitrogen once fruit sets
Ficus carica.fertilizer: Granular balanced fertilizer; compost top-dressing works well
Ficus carica.schedule: 3 times a year: early spring, early summer, midsummer. Stop by August so new growth hardens off
tips: Too much nitrogen gives lush leaves but little fruit
Potted figs need feeding monthly during the growing season
Mulch with compost each spring
Ficus carica.watering: Deeply once a week in summer; potted figs every 2-3 days in heat
Ficus carica.temperature: Fruits best at 20-30 °C; hardy to about -10 °C when dormant
Ficus carica.humidity: Tolerates dry air well; soil should dry slightly between waterings

Solanum tuberosum.npk: Higher phosphorus and potassium, moderate nitrogen (e.g., 5-10-10)
Solanum tuberosum.fertilizer: Granular vegetable fertilizer worked into the soil at planting
Solanum tuberosum.schedule: At planting, then side-dress when plants are 15-20 cm tall and again at flowering (tuber set)
tips: Avoid fresh manure and excess nitrogen - you get leaves instead of tubers
Potassium is key for tuber size and storage quality
Hill soil around stems as plants grow
Solanum tuberosum.watering: 2-3 cm of water per week; most critical while tubers are forming
Solanum tuberosum.temperature: Grows best at 15-21 °C; tuber formation stalls above 27 °C
Solanum tuberosum.humidity: Keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged; dry spells cause knobby tubers

Solanum.npk: Start balanced, then low nitrogen and high phosphorus-potassium at flowering (e.g., 3-4-6 or tomato food)
Solanum.fertilizer: Tomato/vegetable fertilizer with calcium to prevent blossom end rot
Solanum.schedule: At transplant, then every 2 weeks once flowering starts
tips: Too much nitrogen = big leafy plants, few fruits
Keep watering even - calcium uptake depends on it
Magnesium (Epsom salt) helps if older leaves yellow between veins
Solanum.watering: Deeply 2-3× a week at the base; never let it swing between bone-dry and soaked
Solanum.temperature: 21-27 °C day, above 13 °C at night; fruit set fails over 32 °C
Solanum.humidity: Moderate (40-70%); keep leaves dry, steady soil moisture prevents blossom end rot

Capsicum.npk: Balanced early (5-5-5), then higher potassium at fruiting (3-5-7)
Capsicum.fertilizer: Tomato/vegetable fertilizer works perfectly for peppers
Capsicum.schedule: At transplant, then every 2-3 weeks during fruiting
tips: Peppers are lighter feeders than tomatoes - half strength is often enough
Excess nitrogen delays fruiting
Capsicum.watering: When the top 3 cm of soil dries — roughly every 2-3 days in summer
Capsicum.temperature: 21-29 °C day, 16-21 °C night; drops below 12 °C stop growth
Capsicum.humidity: Moderate (50-70%); even moisture, slight drying before harvest concentrates heat

Cucumis.npk: Balanced at planting (5-5-5), higher potassium once vines run (e.g., 3-4-6)
Cucumis.fertilizer: Compost-rich soil plus liquid vegetable feed
Cucumis.schedule: At planting, when vines start to run, and when flowering begins
tips: Heavy feeders and heavy drinkers - never let them dry out
Side-dress with compost mid-season
Cucumis.watering: Heavy and frequent — 3-5 cm per week, daily in hot spells; always at the base
Cucumis.temperature: 24-29 °C; growth stops below 15 °C, frost kills instantly
Cucumis.humidity: High soil moisture at all times; dry spells make cucumbers bitter

Cucurbita.npk: Balanced early, then high potassium for fruiting (e.g., 4-4-8)
Cucurbita.fertilizer: Compost or well-rotted manure at planting plus granular vegetable feed
Cucurbita.schedule: At planting, at first flowers, and monthly while fruiting
tips: Among the heaviest feeders in the garden - plant into a compost-enriched mound
Water at the base to avoid powdery mildew
Cucurbita.watering: Deeply 1-2× a week (2-5 cm); morning watering at the base only
Cucurbita.humidity: Moist soil, dry leaves — wet foliage invites powdery mildew

Lactuca.npk: Nitrogen-forward for leafy growth (e.g., 10-5-5 or fish emulsion)
Lactuca.fertilizer: Liquid fish emulsion or balanced soluble feed at half strength
Lactuca.schedule: Light feed every 2 weeks; lettuce grows fast and shallow
tips: Fast nitrogen keeps leaves tender and sweet
Stop feeding a week before harvest
Lactuca.watering: Light and frequent — shallow roots want moisture every 1-2 days in warmth
Lactuca.temperature: Crisp and sweet at 10-21 °C; bolts bitter above 24 °C
Lactuca.humidity: Constantly moist (not soggy) soil; mulch keeps roots cool

Spinacia.fertilizer: Fish emulsion, blood meal, or balanced soluble feed
Spinacia.schedule: At planting and again when plants have 4-6 true leaves
tips: Spinach bolts under stress - steady nitrogen and water keep it leafy
Likes more neutral soil than most vegetables
Spinacia.watering: Keep evenly moist; 2-3 cm per week, more in warm spells
Spinacia.temperature: Thrives at 10-21 °C; heat above 24 °C triggers bolting
Spinacia.humidity: Steady soil moisture; drought stress means instant bolting

Brassica.npk: Nitrogen-forward with steady everything (e.g., 8-4-4), plus boron and calcium
Brassica.fertilizer: Balanced granular at planting, nitrogen side-dress later
Brassica.schedule: At planting, then side-dress 3-4 weeks in; broccoli again when heads start forming
tips: Heavy feeders - poor soil gives small, bitter heads
Lime acidic soil before planting
Brassica.watering: 2-3 cm per week, consistent; heads crack if soaked after a dry spell
Brassica.temperature: Cool-season crop: 15-21 °C ideal; mature plants shrug off light frost
Brassica.humidity: Even soil moisture throughout; mulch heavily

Allium.npk: Nitrogen early for leaves (they become bulb layers), none after bulbing starts
Allium.fertilizer: Blood meal or ammonium sulfate side-dress in spring
Allium.schedule: Every 2-3 weeks until bulbs begin to swell, then stop completely
tips: Every leaf equals a ring on the bulb - push leafy growth early
Late nitrogen delays bulbing and hurts storage
Allium.watering: Weekly while leaves grow; STOP watering once bulbs mature and tops flop
Allium.temperature: Leaves grow at 13-24 °C; bulbing is triggered by day length, not heat
Allium.humidity: Moist spring, dry finish — wet soil at maturity rots stored bulbs

Daucus.npk: Low nitrogen, higher phosphorus and potassium (e.g., 1-2-2)
Daucus.fertilizer: Compost worked deep; avoid fresh manure entirely
Daucus.schedule: Little needed if soil is decent; one light feed when tops are 10 cm
tips: Fresh manure and lumpy soil cause forked, hairy roots
Loose, deep, stone-free soil matters more than fertilizer
Daucus.watering: Evenly moist while germinating; then 2-3 cm per week — splitting follows feast-or-famine watering
Daucus.temperature: Best flavor grown at 15-21 °C; sweetens after light fall frost
Daucus.humidity: Steady moderate moisture in deep, loose soil

Phaseolus.npk: Low nitrogen - beans fix their own. Phosphorus and potassium only (e.g., 1-4-4)
Phaseolus.fertilizer: Compost at planting is usually all they need
Phaseolus.schedule: At planting; optionally once at flowering
tips: Added nitrogen makes beans lazy - all vine, few pods
Inoculant powder helps in soil that has never grown beans
Phaseolus.watering: 2-3 cm per week, most important during flowering and pod fill
Phaseolus.temperature: Sow in soil above 16 °C; grows best at 18-27 °C
Phaseolus.humidity: Moderate; don't work among wet plants — it spreads disease

Pisum.fertilizer: Compost at planting; peas largely feed themselves
Pisum.schedule: At planting only, in most soils
tips: Like beans, peas fix nitrogen - skip the nitrogen fertilizer
Wood ash gives a gentle potassium boost
Pisum.watering: Light until flowering, then steady — 2-3 cm per week during pod fill
Pisum.temperature: A cool-weather crop: 13-18 °C; quits producing above 27 °C
Pisum.humidity: Even moisture; mulch to keep spring roots cool

Zea.npk: Very nitrogen-hungry (e.g., 16-4-8 or regular nitrogen side-dressing)
Zea.fertilizer: Balanced at planting, then nitrogen (blood meal, urea, fish emulsion) later
Zea.schedule: At planting, when knee-high, and at tasseling
tips: Pale green leaves mean it wants nitrogen now
Plant in blocks, not rows, for pollination
Zea.watering: 2-3 cm per week; critical at tasseling and ear fill — drought then costs kernels
Zea.humidity: Deep soil moisture during silking; shallow daily sprinkles do little

Beta.npk: Balanced with decent potassium (e.g., 5-5-8), plus boron
tips: Black dead spots inside beets usually mean boron deficiency
Excess nitrogen makes tops at the expense of roots
Beta.watering: 2-3 cm per week, steady; woody roots follow drought stress
Beta.temperature: 15-21 °C ideal; tolerates light frost both ends of the season

Fragaria.npk: Balanced (10-10-10) after harvest; light feeding in spring
Fragaria.schedule: Light feed in early spring, main feed right after harvest (that's when next year's buds form)
tips: Heavy spring nitrogen gives soft, bland berries
Renovate and feed June-bearers immediately after picking
Fragaria.watering: 2-3 cm per week; daily lightly during fruiting in heat (shallow roots)
Fragaria.temperature: 15-26 °C; flowers are frost-tender — cover on cold nights
Fragaria.humidity: Moist soil, dry berries: straw mulch keeps fruit off wet ground

Rubus.fertilizer: Granular balanced feed plus compost mulch
Rubus.schedule: Early spring as growth starts; everbearers again in early summer
tips: Feed the rows, not the plants - roots spread widely
Mulch heavily; brambles love cool, rich root zones
Rubus.watering: 2-5 cm per week from bloom through harvest
Rubus.temperature: Canes hardy to -20 °C or lower; fruit best at 18-24 °C
Rubus.humidity: Cool, moist, mulched root zone; good airflow through the canes

Vaccinium.npk: Acid-formula fertilizer (e.g., azalea food, ammonium sulfate based)
Vaccinium.fertilizer: Holly-tone / azalea fertilizer; never use nitrate-based feeds
Vaccinium.schedule: Early spring and again 6 weeks later; nothing after July
tips: Yellow leaves with green veins = soil not acidic enough, not lack of feed
Acidify with elemental sulfur months before planting
Mulch with pine needles or pine bark
Vaccinium.watering: 2-5 cm per week; shallow fine roots dry out fast — never let them
Vaccinium.temperature: Hardy; fruits best at 18-26 °C (check chill-hour needs for your variety)
Vaccinium.humidity: Constantly moist (not flooded) acidic soil; pine-needle mulch is ideal

Vitis.npk: Low and lean - balanced feed only if growth is weak (e.g., light 10-10-10)
Vitis.fertilizer: Compost; grapes on fertile soil usually need nothing
Vitis.schedule: Once in early spring, only if shoots grew under 1 m last year
tips: Overfed vines make jungle canopy and poor fruit
Potassium deficiency shows as browning leaf edges mid-summer
Vitis.watering: Deep and infrequent once established; ease off near harvest to concentrate sugars
Vitis.temperature: Growing season at 15-32 °C; dormant vines take hard frost
Vitis.humidity: Prefers dry air — humid canopies get fungal disease; prune for airflow

Citrus.npk: Nitrogen-rich citrus formula with micronutrients (e.g., 6-3-3 plus iron, zinc, manganese)
Citrus.fertilizer: Dedicated citrus food - citrus are prone to micronutrient deficiencies
Citrus.schedule: Every 6 weeks spring through summer; monthly for potted trees; little in winter
tips: Yellow leaves with green veins = iron or manganese deficiency, common in pots
Potted citrus leach nutrients fast - feed little and often
Water deeply before feeding, never feed dry soil
Citrus.watering: Deeply when the top 5 cm dries; potted trees roughly weekly, never standing in water
Citrus.temperature: 13-30 °C; most types damaged below -2 °C — bring pots in before frost
Citrus.humidity: Moderate to high (50%+); indoor winter air is too dry — mist or use a pebble tray

Malus.npk: Balanced (10-10-10) only while young; mature trees often need just nitrogen, judged by growth
Malus.fertilizer: Granular balanced feed spread to the drip line
Malus.schedule: Early spring before bloom; skip feeding if shoots grew more than 30 cm last year
tips: Overfeeding causes watersprouts and fire-blight-prone soft growth
Never fertilize after July
Malus.watering: Young trees weekly and deeply; established trees only in drought
Malus.temperature: Cold-hardy; needs winter chill (varies by variety) to fruit well
Malus.humidity: Average; prune the crown open so leaves dry quickly

Prunus.npk: Low nitrogen balanced feed (e.g., 5-10-10); peaches slightly more nitrogen
Prunus.fertilizer: Granular fruit tree fertilizer at the drip line
Prunus.schedule: Once in early spring; young trees a second light feed in late May
tips: Judge by growth: 25-40 cm of new shoot per year is right for mature trees
Excess nitrogen worsens brown rot and canker
Prunus.watering: Deeply every 1-2 weeks in dry weather, especially while fruit swells
Prunus.temperature: Hardy, but early blooms are frost-vulnerable; fruits at 18-27 °C
Prunus.humidity: Average; avoid wetting foliage — this family rots easily

Pyrus.npk: Very low nitrogen (e.g., 5-10-10) - pears are fire blight magnets
Pyrus.fertilizer: Light granular feed, or just compost mulch
Pyrus.schedule: Once in early spring, and only if growth was weak
tips: Lush nitrogen-fed growth is exactly what fire blight attacks
When in doubt, don't feed a pear
Pyrus.watering: Deeply every 1-2 weeks in drought; established trees are tough
Pyrus.temperature: Cold-hardy; needs some winter chill; fruit ripens best at 18-24 °C

Persea.npk: Citrus/avocado formula with nitrogen and zinc (e.g., 6-3-3 + micros)
Persea.schedule: Every 6-8 weeks during the growing season; sparingly the first year
tips: Extremely sensitive to salt buildup - flush pots regularly
Needs perfect drainage; root rot kills more avocados than hunger
Persea.watering: Deeply, then let the top 5-10 cm dry — soggy roots are fatal to avocados
Persea.humidity: Moderate to high; mulch thickly but keep it off the trunk

Musa.fertilizer: High-potassium feed or dedicated banana/palm fertilizer
Musa.schedule: Monthly while warm; bananas eat constantly in summer
tips: One of the hungriest plants you can grow - compost generously
Potassium drives fruit size and cold resilience
Musa.watering: Constantly thirsty in warmth — every 1-2 days in summer; huge leaves transpire a lot
Musa.temperature: Loves 24-32 °C; growth stops below 14 °C, foliage dies at frost
Musa.humidity: High (60%+); indoor bananas appreciate misting and grouped plants

Olea.npk: Modest nitrogen (e.g., light 10-5-5); olives tolerate lean soil
Olea.schedule: Early spring and early summer, lightly
tips: Olives fruit better slightly stressed than pampered
Perfect drainage beats any fertilizer
Olea.watering: Drought-tough once established; deep soak monthly in dry summers, weekly for pots
Olea.temperature: Mediterranean: hot dry summers, cool winters; damaged below about -10 °C
Olea.humidity: Low to moderate; hates humid, waterlogged conditions

Ocimum.npk: Light balanced feed (e.g., 5-5-5 at half strength)
Ocimum.fertilizer: Diluted liquid feed or fish emulsion
Ocimum.schedule: Every 3-4 weeks; potted basil every 2 weeks
tips: Overfed basil grows big but loses flavor - oils concentrate in leaner plants
Pinch flowers to keep leaves coming
Ocimum.watering: When the surface dries — every 2-3 days in summer, daily for small pots
Ocimum.temperature: Warmth-lover: 18-30 °C; sulks below 10 °C, blackens at frost
Ocimum.humidity: Evenly moist soil; morning watering at the base

Mentha.npk: Barely any - light balanced feed if leaves pale
tips: Mint thrives on neglect; feeding mostly makes it more invasive
Grow in a pot unless you want a mint lawn
Mentha.watering: Keep moist — mint is the rare herb that likes wet feet a little
Mentha.temperature: Grows at 13-25 °C; dies back in frost, returns from roots
Mentha.humidity: Moist soil and partial shade keep it lush

Salvia.npk: Very light - a little compost in spring
Salvia.fertilizer: Compost only; skip commercial fertilizer in the ground
tips: Mediterranean herbs get leggy and bland when overfed
Sharp drainage matters far more than nutrients
Salvia.watering: Only when soil is dry 3-5 cm down; established plants handle drought
Salvia.temperature: 18-29 °C; most garden sages are hardy to around -15 °C
Salvia.humidity: Low; dry air and sharp drainage, Mediterranean style

Rosmarinus.npk: Minimal - light balanced feed for potted plants only
Rosmarinus.fertilizer: Compost or quarter-strength liquid feed for pots
Rosmarinus.schedule: Spring only; potted plants 2-3 times a season
tips: Rosemary evolved on rocky hillsides - lean and dry is happy
Overwatering kills it long before underfeeding does
Rosmarinus.watering: Sparingly — let pots dry well between waterings; overwatering is the #1 killer
Rosmarinus.temperature: 18-29 °C; many varieties damaged below -7 °C — pot and shelter in cold climates
Rosmarinus.humidity: Low; loathes humid stagnant air and wet winter soil

Thymus.npk: Minimal; none in decent garden soil
Thymus.fertilizer: A dusting of compost in spring at most
tips: Rich soil makes thyme floppy and weak-flavored
Gritty, fast-draining soil is the real fertilizer
Thymus.watering: Rarely — only prolonged drought bothers established thyme
Thymus.temperature: Hardy little shrub; thrives in 15-30 °C summers
Thymus.humidity: Low; gritty dry soil, full sun

Petroselinum.fertilizer: Fish emulsion or half-strength balanced liquid
tips: Parsley is hungrier than most herbs - it's grown for lush leaves
Cut outer stems first to keep it producing
Petroselinum.watering: Evenly moist — about 2-3 cm per week; wilts dramatically but recovers

Coriandrum.schedule: Once or twice during its short life
tips: Heat, not hunger, makes cilantro bolt - succession sow instead of overfeeding
Keep soil evenly moist
Coriandrum.watering: Keep evenly moist; dry + hot = instant bolting
Coriandrum.humidity: Moist soil, cool position; succession-sow rather than fight summer

Lavandula.npk: Essentially none - lavender prefers poor soil
Lavandula.fertilizer: None, or a little compost at planting. No mulch against the stem
tips: Fertilizer reduces fragrance and winter hardiness
Add lime to acidic soil; gravel mulch beats bark
Lavandula.watering: Very little once established; water young plants until rooted, then mostly leave alone
Lavandula.temperature: 15-30 °C summers; English lavender hardy to about -15 °C
Lavandula.humidity: Low — humidity plus wet soil kills more lavender than cold ever does

Rosa.npk: Balanced with extra phosphorus and potassium (e.g., 4-6-4 or dedicated rose food)
Rosa.fertilizer: Rose food or alfalfa meal plus compost; liquid feed between flushes of bloom
Rosa.schedule: First feed when leaves open in spring, then after each bloom flush; stop 6-8 weeks before first frost
tips: Repeat-blooming roses are heavy feeders
Banana peels and alfalfa are classic potassium boosters
Late-season feeding produces frost-tender growth
Rosa.watering: Deeply 1-2× a week at the base (more in pots); shallow sprinkles grow shallow roots
Rosa.temperature: Blooms best at 15-26 °C; hardiness varies — mound mulch over grafts in cold winters
Rosa.humidity: Average; water in the morning and keep foliage dry to hold off black spot

Hydrangea.npk: Balanced slow-release (e.g., 10-10-10); for blue flowers use low-phosphorus acid feed
Hydrangea.schedule: Once in spring, optionally again in early summer; nothing after July
tips: Flower color follows pH: aluminum sulfate for blue, garden lime for pink (bigleaf types only)
High phosphorus blocks aluminum uptake and keeps flowers pink
Overfeeding gives leaves instead of blooms
Hydrangea.watering: Thirsty — deeply 2-3× a week in heat; wilting by afternoon is its signature complaint
Hydrangea.temperature: Happiest at 15-25 °C with afternoon shade; buds of bigleaf types freeze below about -15 °C
Hydrangea.humidity: Moist, mulched, cool root zone; moderate to high air humidity

Rhododendron.npk: Acid-formula feed (e.g., azalea/camellia food, 4-3-4 with sulfur)
Rhododendron.schedule: Right after flowering, lightly; nothing after mid-summer
tips: Shallow fine roots burn easily - always underfeed rather than overfeed
Yellowing between veins means pH is too high
Mulch with pine bark instead of feeding more
Rhododendron.watering: Keep shallow roots evenly moist — weekly deep watering plus permanent mulch
Rhododendron.temperature: Cool-climate shrub: 13-24 °C; most are quite cold-hardy
Rhododendron.humidity: Moderate to high; hates hot dry wind

Camellia.fertilizer: Acid fertilizer plus pine bark mulch
Camellia.schedule: After bloom ends, then 6-8 weeks later; never while flowering
tips: Feeding during bud set can cause bud drop
Camellias are light feeders - half the label rate is safer
Camellia.watering: Evenly moist, never soggy; extra care with water while buds are forming (summer-fall)
Camellia.temperature: Mild-climate: 7-21 °C preferred; flowers damaged below about -5 °C
Camellia.humidity: Moderate to high; sheltered from drying wind

Gardenia.npk: Acid formula with iron (e.g., 3-1-2 acid feed + chelated iron)
Gardenia.fertilizer: Azalea food; chelated iron spray for yellowing leaves
Gardenia.schedule: Every 4-6 weeks spring to late summer
tips: Gardenias are the drama queens of acid-lovers - yellow leaves usually mean iron lockout from high pH
Bud drop is from temperature and water swings, not hunger
Gardenia.watering: Evenly moist with room-temperature (ideally soft) water; never bone-dry
Gardenia.temperature: Fussy: 18-24 °C day and crucially 15-18 °C nights to set buds
Gardenia.humidity: High (50-60%+); dry indoor air = yellow leaves and dropped buds

Paeonia.fertilizer: Bulb food or low-N granular around (not on) the crown
Paeonia.schedule: Early spring when shoots are 10 cm, and again after flowering
tips: Nitrogen-fed peonies flop and skip blooming
Planting depth (eyes 3-5 cm deep max) affects bloom more than any fertilizer
Paeonia.watering: Deeply every 10-14 days in dry weather; established peonies are drought-tolerant
Paeonia.temperature: Needs cold winters (chilling) to bloom; grows at 15-26 °C
Paeonia.humidity: Average; airflow around stems prevents botrytis

Dahlia.npk: Low nitrogen, high potassium (e.g., 5-10-10 or tomato food)
Dahlia.fertilizer: Tomato fertilizer is the classic dahlia feed
Dahlia.schedule: Monthly from a month after planting until early autumn
tips: High nitrogen gives giant plants, weak stems, few flowers, and rot-prone tubers
Stop feeding in September to help tubers cure
Dahlia.watering: None until sprouts show, then deeply 2-3× a week in bloom
Dahlia.temperature: Grows at 16-24 °C; tubers die in frozen ground — lift them in cold climates

Tulipa.npk: Bulb food / bone meal at planting; balanced feed as leaves emerge
Tulipa.fertilizer: Bulb fertilizer worked into the planting hole
Tulipa.schedule: At fall planting, then once when shoots emerge in spring
tips: Feed the leaves after bloom - that's next year's flower being built
Never cut leaves until they yellow naturally
Tulipa.watering: Water at planting and in dry springs; keep DRY in summer dormancy
Tulipa.temperature: Needs 12-16 weeks below 10 °C in winter; blooms at 10-18 °C
Tulipa.humidity: Well-drained always — wet summer soil rots bulbs

Narcissus.npk: Bulb food at planting, low-N feed (e.g., 5-10-12) as foliage emerges
Narcissus.schedule: At fall planting and at spring emergence; after-bloom feed helps naturalizing
tips: Let foliage die back naturally for 6 weeks after bloom
High nitrogen encourages bulb rot
Narcissus.watering: Moist fall through spring; dry rest in summer
Narcissus.temperature: Cold-hardy; needs winter chill; blooms at 10-18 °C

Lilium.schedule: When shoots emerge and again at flowering
tips: Lilies like their heads in sun and feet in cool, mulched soil
Leave stems standing after bloom to feed the bulb
Lilium.watering: 2-3 cm per week while growing; bulbs never want to sit in water
Lilium.temperature: Blooms at 18-24 °C; likes cool mulched roots and sunny tops

Chrysanthemum.npk: Balanced feed (e.g., 5-5-5) until buds show color, then stop
Chrysanthemum.schedule: Monthly from spring until buds color up
tips: Pinch tips until early July for bushy plants
Feeding while blooming shortens flower life
Chrysanthemum.watering: Evenly moist — shallow roots wilt fast in pots; daily checks in fall heat
Chrysanthemum.temperature: 15-24 °C; blooming is triggered by long nights, not temperature
Chrysanthemum.humidity: Moderate; water the soil, not the dense flower canopy

Petunia.npk: Steady balanced feed with iron (e.g., 20-10-20); they are famously hungry
Petunia.fertilizer: Water-soluble feed; slow-release pellets in baskets as a base
Petunia.schedule: Every 1-2 weeks in beds, weekly in baskets and pots
tips: Yellowing new growth means iron deficiency - common in petunias
Hanging baskets wash nutrients out with every watering, so feed often
Petunia.watering: Beds: weekly deep. Baskets: daily in summer, twice on scorchers
Petunia.humidity: Moderate; baskets dry brutally fast in wind

tips: Overfed geraniums make leaves, not flowers
Deadhead religiously for continuous bloom
Pelargonium.watering: Let the top few cm dry between waterings — slightly dry beats soggy
Pelargonium.temperature: 16-27 °C day; bring indoors before frost (they overwinter easily)
Pelargonium.humidity: Low to moderate; tolerates dry air well

Tagetes.npk: Light balanced feed; marigolds prefer lean soil
Tagetes.fertilizer: Compost at planting is usually enough
Tagetes.schedule: One light feed a month after planting, if at all
tips: Rich soil gives lush foliage and few flowers
They genuinely do better slightly starved
Tagetes.watering: Weekly deep watering; established marigolds handle dry spells
Tagetes.temperature: 18-30 °C; frost-tender but otherwise unbothered by heat
Tagetes.humidity: Low to moderate; overhead water spoils the blooms

Helianthus.npk: Balanced at planting, nitrogen while growing, potassium at bud stage
Helianthus.fertilizer: Compost-rich soil plus a granular balanced feed
Helianthus.schedule: At planting and once when half grown
tips: Giant varieties are heavy feeders and drinkers
Too much nitrogen late = weak stems that snap
Helianthus.watering: Deeply weekly — taproots reach far, but giants drink heavily near bloom
Helianthus.temperature: 21-29 °C; seedlings take light frost, mature plants shrug off heat
Helianthus.humidity: Moderate soil moisture; staking + wet soil + wind = toppled giants

Viola.schedule: Every 2-3 weeks while blooming; monthly in cool weather
tips: Pansies feed and bloom even in cool seasons - don't stop in fall
Deadhead to keep flowers coming
Viola.watering: Evenly moist; morning watering every 2-3 days in mild weather
Viola.temperature: Cool-lovers: 7-18 °C; flower through frosts, melt in summer heat
Viola.humidity: Moist cool soil; mulch in warm spells

Impatiens.npk: Light balanced feed (e.g., 10-10-10 at half strength)
Impatiens.schedule: Every 2 weeks in pots, monthly in beds
tips: Overfeeding gives tall leafy plants with sparse flowers
Consistent moisture matters more than food
Impatiens.watering: Frequently — wilts theatrically when thirsty; daily in warm shade pots
Impatiens.temperature: 18-24 °C; among the first killed by frost
Impatiens.humidity: Moderate to high; consistently moist soil

Fuchsia.npk: Steady dilute balanced feed (e.g., quarter-strength every watering)
Fuchsia.fertilizer: Water-soluble balanced or slightly high-K feed
Fuchsia.schedule: Weakly, weekly - the classic fuchsia rule
tips: Constant light feeding beats occasional heavy doses
Stop feeding hard in autumn to let plants rest
Fuchsia.watering: Keep baskets evenly moist — daily in summer; never bone-dry
Fuchsia.temperature: Cool performer: 13-24 °C; drops buds in heat above 27 °C
Fuchsia.humidity: High; loves cool, humid, bright shade

Begonia.npk: Dilute balanced feed (e.g., 10-10-10 at quarter strength)
tips: Begonia roots burn easily - always dilute more than the label says
Tuberous types: stop feeding in late summer
Begonia.watering: When the surface dries; water at the base — fleshy stems rot when splashed
Begonia.temperature: 18-24 °C; tuberous types need lifting before frost
Begonia.humidity: Moderate to high air humidity, but soil on the drier side of moist

Hibiscus.npk: High potassium, moderate nitrogen, LOW phosphorus (e.g., 12-4-18 or 10-4-12)
Hibiscus.fertilizer: Hibiscus food or high-K feed; avoid bloom boosters
Hibiscus.schedule: Every 2 weeks in summer, monthly in spring/fall, none in winter
tips: Hibiscus is unusual: phosphorus actually builds up and poisons it over time
Skip the 'super bloom' high-P fertilizers entirely
Hibiscus.watering: Daily in hot weather for pots — huge drinker in bloom; less in winter
Hibiscus.temperature: Tropical types: 16-32 °C, indoors below 10 °C; hardy types take -20 °C
Hibiscus.humidity: Moderate to high; dry air plus dry soil = bud drop

Bougainvillea.npk: Balanced with micronutrients (e.g., 6-8-10 + iron); lean feeding promotes bloom
tips: Blooms best slightly stressed - a little hunger and drought triggers color
Overwatering plus overfeeding = all green, no bracts
Bougainvillea.watering: Deeply, then let it dry properly — mild drought triggers the color show
Bougainvillea.temperature: Loves 18-35 °C; leaves drop below 5 °C, frost kills
Bougainvillea.humidity: Low to moderate; blooms best treated a little mean

Jasminum.npk: Balanced feed with a potassium lean (e.g., 7-9-5)
Jasminum.schedule: Every 2-4 weeks during the growing season
tips: Potassium supports flowering and fragrance
Root-bound potted jasmine blooms better - don't over-pot
Jasminum.watering: Evenly moist in growth and bloom; slightly drier in winter rest
Jasminum.temperature: 16-27 °C; many need cool (10-13 °C) autumn nights to set buds
Jasminum.humidity: Moderate to high; mist indoor plants in winter

Clematis.npk: Low nitrogen bloom feed (e.g., 5-10-10 or rose/tomato food)
Clematis.schedule: Spring when buds swell, then monthly; pause while actually flowering
tips: The old rule holds: head in the sun, feet in the shade - mulch the roots
Feeding during bloom can shorten the display
Clematis.watering: Deeply weekly — 'head in the sun, feet in the shade' includes moist, mulched roots
Clematis.temperature: Hardy; grows best at 15-25 °C with cool roots
Clematis.humidity: Moderate; mulch or underplant to shade the root zone

Hosta.schedule: Once in spring as leaves unfurl; optional light feed in early summer; none after July
tips: Hostas are mostly fed by rich, moist soil - compost beats fertilizer
Late feeding delays dormancy and invites frost damage
Hosta.watering: 2-3 cm per week; big-leaved varieties in dry shade need more than you think
Hosta.temperature: Cool shade plant: 10-24 °C; fully hardy, needs winter cold to rest
Hosta.humidity: Moist rich soil; crispy edges mean thirst or too much sun

Syringa.npk: Minimal - a little balanced feed only in poor soil; likes lime
Syringa.fertilizer: Compost; a handful of garden lime in acidic soil
tips: Fertilized lilacs often refuse to bloom - lean soil and full sun work better
Prune right after flowering, not later
Syringa.watering: Only in real drought once established; new shrubs weekly for a season
Syringa.temperature: Cold-climate shrub — needs freezing winters to bloom well
Syringa.humidity: Average; airflow fends off powdery mildew

Magnolia.schedule: Early spring for young trees; established trees rarely need feeding
tips: Shallow fleshy roots - never dig fertilizer in, just surface-spread and water
Mulch wide, not deep
Magnolia.watering: Young trees deeply weekly for 2 seasons; mature trees only in drought
Magnolia.temperature: Varies by species; early bloomers lose flowers to late frost — site carefully
Magnolia.humidity: Moist, mulched root zone; shallow roots resent disturbance

Acer.npk: Low and slow - light slow-release in spring if growth is weak (e.g., half-rate 10-10-10)
Acer.fertilizer: Compost mulch is usually all a maple wants
Acer.schedule: Early spring only, and only young or weak trees
tips: Japanese maples hate heavy feeding - it causes coarse growth and leaf scorch
Never fertilize a newly planted maple its first year
Acer.watering: Japanese maples: evenly moist, never waterlogged; big maples: only young trees need help
Acer.temperature: Hardy; Japanese maple leaves scorch above 32 °C in sun and wind
Acer.humidity: Moderate; sheltered from hot dry wind to keep leaf tips green

Buxus.fertilizer: Granular shrub feed at the drip line
Buxus.schedule: Early spring; a second light feed in fall is okay in mild climates
tips: Bronze winter foliage often signals nitrogen hunger
Shallow roots: surface feed, never dig it in
Buxus.watering: Deeply every 1-2 weeks in dry spells; shallow roots under mulch
Buxus.temperature: Hardy; winter sun + frozen ground causes bronzing

Ficus.category: Ficus (rubber plant, fiddle-leaf fig, weeping fig)
Ficus.npk: Nitrogen-leaning foliage feed (e.g., 3-1-2 ratio houseplant food)
Ficus.fertilizer: Liquid houseplant fertilizer at half strength
Ficus.schedule: Monthly spring through early fall; nothing in winter
tips: Fiddle-leaf figs prefer consistency - same spot, same schedule
Flush the pot with plain water every few months to clear salt buildup
Ficus.watering: When the top 3-5 cm dries — typically weekly indoors; less in winter
Ficus.temperature: 16-27 °C; hates cold drafts and sudden moves (cue leaf drop)
Ficus.humidity: Moderate (40-60%); wipe dusty leaves so they can breathe

Monstera.fertilizer: Liquid houseplant feed at half strength
Monstera.schedule: Monthly during spring/summer growth; every 2 months or none in winter
tips: Big fenestrated leaves come from light and age more than fertilizer
Pale new leaves = feed; brown crispy edges = probably overfed or dry air
Monstera.watering: When the top 5 cm dries — roughly every 1-2 weeks; less in winter
Monstera.humidity: Happiest at 60%+, tolerates 40%; loves a moss pole and an occasional shower

Epipremnum.npk: Any balanced houseplant feed, diluted (e.g., 10-10-10 at half strength)
Epipremnum.schedule: Monthly in growing season; pothos tolerates neglect
tips: One of the hardest plants to underfeed - when in doubt, skip it
Feed only when actively putting out new leaves
Epipremnum.watering: Let the top half of the pot dry; droopy leaves tell you it's time
Epipremnum.humidity: Unfussy — average room humidity is fine

Philodendron.fertilizer: Liquid houseplant feed at half strength
Philodendron.schedule: Monthly spring-summer, every 6-8 weeks in winter if growing
tips: Small new leaves on a mature plant usually mean it's hungry
Salt-sensitive - flush the pot occasionally
Philodendron.watering: When the top 3-5 cm dries; yellow leaves usually mean too much water

Dracaena.npk: Light balanced feed (e.g., 10-10-10 at quarter strength)
Dracaena.schedule: Every 1-2 months in growing season only
tips: Very fluoride-sensitive: brown leaf tips often come from tap water and perlite, not hunger
Overfeeding shows as burnt tips and pale streaks
Dracaena.watering: Every 10-14 days — let the top half dry; use filtered/rain water if tips brown
Dracaena.humidity: Average room humidity is fine; brown tips are usually water quality, not dryness

Sansevieria.npk: Minimal - cactus feed at half strength (e.g., 2-7-7 diluted)
Sansevieria.schedule: 2-3 times a year during warm months is plenty
tips: Snake plants store everything - feeding more does nothing but risk root burn
Never feed in winter or right after repotting
Sansevieria.watering: Every 2-6 weeks — only when soil is fully dry; monthly or less in winter
Sansevieria.humidity: Low; thrives in dry air where other plants sulk

Chlorophytum.npk: Dilute balanced feed (e.g., 10-10-10 at quarter to half strength)
tips: Brown tips are usually fluoride/salts - use rainwater or distilled, and go easy on feed
Overfed spider plants stop making babies
Chlorophytum.watering: Weekly-ish, letting the top few cm dry; fleshy roots store a reserve
Chlorophytum.humidity: Average; browning tips point at tap-water fluoride before dryness

Spathiphyllum.npk: Dilute balanced feed (e.g., 20-20-20 at quarter strength)
tips: Green flowers mean too much fertilizer
Brown tips mean salts or chlorinated water - flush the pot
Spathiphyllum.watering: When it droops slightly or the top 3 cm dries — about weekly; perks up within hours
Spathiphyllum.humidity: Moderate to high; brown tips in dry rooms

Zamioculcas.npk: Minimal - balanced feed at quarter strength
Zamioculcas.schedule: 2-3 times a year, growing season only
tips: ZZ plants run on stored energy in their rhizomes - they barely need you
Overfeeding and overwatering are the only real ways to kill one
Zamioculcas.watering: Every 2-4 weeks, fully dry between; when in doubt, wait a week
Zamioculcas.humidity: Low; dry air is no problem at all

Goeppertia.fertilizer: Gentle liquid feed; they are salt-sensitive divas
Goeppertia.schedule: Monthly in growing season at quarter strength
tips: Calatheas burn from fertilizer salts easily - less is more
Crispy edges are almost always water quality or humidity, not hunger
Goeppertia.watering: Keep lightly moist (never soggy) with rain/distilled water; small sips often
Goeppertia.humidity: High (60%+) — the non-negotiable part of owning a calathea

Calathea.fertilizer: Gentle liquid feed; they are salt-sensitive divas
Calathea.schedule: Monthly in growing season at quarter strength
tips: Calatheas burn from fertilizer salts easily - less is more
Crispy edges are almost always water quality or humidity, not hunger
Calathea.watering: Keep lightly moist (never soggy) with rain/distilled water; small sips often
Calathea.humidity: High (60%+) — the non-negotiable part of owning a calathea

Hedera.fertilizer: Liquid houseplant feed indoors; nothing needed outdoors
Hedera.schedule: Monthly indoors in growing season; outdoor ivy needs none
tips: Don't feed ivy in hot midsummer or cold winter - it pauses growth then
Outdoor ivy fed regularly becomes even more invasive
Hedera.watering: When the top 3 cm dries; ivy prefers slightly dry to slightly wet
Hedera.temperature: 10-21 °C — cooler than most houseplants like it; hardy outdoors
Hedera.humidity: Moderate; hot dry rooms invite spider mites

Hoya.npk: Light balanced feed, switch to higher phosphorus when budding (e.g., 5-10-5)
Hoya.fertilizer: Dilute liquid feed or orchid food
Hoya.schedule: Monthly in growth; stop in winter
tips: Never remove the old flower spurs - they rebloom from the same spot
Slightly root-bound hoyas flower best
Hoya.watering: Let it dry well between waterings — semi-succulent leaves hold reserves

Peperomia.schedule: Monthly at most in growing season
tips: Tiny root systems - they feed lightly by design
Overwatering is the killer; feeding is almost optional
Peperomia.watering: When the top half dries — about every 10 days; overwatering is the main killer
Peperomia.humidity: Average rooms suit them; thick leaves buffer dry spells

Saintpaulia.npk: Dedicated violet food (e.g., 14-12-14) or balanced feed at quarter strength
Saintpaulia.fertilizer: African violet fertilizer, every watering at low dose
Saintpaulia.schedule: Quarter strength with each watering, or monthly at half strength
tips: Water from below to keep leaves dry
No blooms usually means not enough light, not too little food
Saintpaulia.watering: From below when the surface dries; room-temperature water, never on the leaves
Saintpaulia.temperature: Steady 18-24 °C; cold windowsills spot the leaves
Saintpaulia.humidity: Moderate to high (50%+); pebble tray, not misting

Phalaenopsis.npk: Orchid food, 'weakly weekly' (e.g., 20-20-20 at quarter strength)
Phalaenopsis.schedule: Quarter strength weekly, plain water every 4th watering to flush
tips: Flush with plain water monthly - orchid roots burn from salt easily
Feed less (or not at all) while in full bloom
Never use regular potting soil for orchids
Phalaenopsis.watering: Weekly-ish: when roots turn silvery, soak and drain fully; never leave water in the crown
Phalaenopsis.temperature: 18-29 °C day; a few weeks of 16-18 °C nights triggers a new flower spike
Phalaenopsis.humidity: 50-70%; bathroom and kitchen windows are orchid real estate

Aloe.npk: Low and rare - cactus feed (e.g., 2-7-7) at half strength
Aloe.schedule: 2-3 times during spring and summer, none otherwise
tips: Overfed aloe grows soft, floppy, and prone to rot
Gritty soil and sun matter infinitely more than fertilizer
Aloe.watering: Deeply, then fully dry — every 2-3 weeks in summer, monthly or less in winter
Aloe.humidity: Low; dry air and gritty soil

Haworthia.npk: Almost none - cactus feed at quarter strength
Haworthia.schedule: Once or twice a year in spring/summer
tips: Slow growers that barely eat - when in doubt, don't feed
Etiolation (stretching) means it wants light, not food
Haworthia.watering: Every 2-3 weeks in growth, scarcely in winter; shriveling leaves = finally time
Haworthia.humidity: Low; tolerates rooms too dim and dry for most succulents

Echeveria.npk: Low nitrogen cactus feed (e.g., 2-7-7) at half strength
tips: Overfeeding ruins the compact rosette shape
Tight form and good color come from bright light and lean soil
Echeveria.watering: Soak and dry — every 10-14 days in summer, monthly in winter; never water the rosette
Echeveria.humidity: Low; humid stagnant air rots the rosette

Crassula.npk: Low - cactus feed at half strength
tips: Jades live decades on almost nothing - lean feeding keeps them sturdy
Feed only established, actively growing plants
Crassula.watering: When leaves lose their gloss or soil is long dry — every 2-3 weeks, less in winter

Kalanchoe.npk: Balanced feed while growing; higher potassium to encourage rebloom
Kalanchoe.fertilizer: Diluted balanced or flowering houseplant feed
Kalanchoe.schedule: Monthly in spring/summer; stop during the short-day rest that triggers blooming
tips: Rebloom needs 6 weeks of long nights, not more fertilizer
Succulent rules apply: well-drained soil, modest feeding
Kalanchoe.watering: Every 1-2 weeks, drying out between; less during the dark winter rest

Sedum.npk: None to minimal - these thrive in poor soil
Sedum.fertilizer: A thin layer of compost at most
Sedum.schedule: Not needed; maybe once in spring for container plants
tips: Fertilized sedums grow tall, floppy, and split open
Lean, gritty, sunny = perfect
Sedum.watering: Almost never once established outdoors; pots monthly in summer
Sedum.temperature: Hardy to deep cold; bakes happily above 30 °C
Sedum.humidity: Low; wet winter soil is the only real enemy

Agave.npk: None in the ground; rare dilute cactus feed in pots
Agave.fertilizer: Cactus fertilizer for potted plants only
Agave.schedule: 1-2 times a year for pots; never for in-ground plants
tips: Feeding an agave can push it to flower - and agaves die after flowering
Seriously: don't fertilize agaves you want to keep
Agave.watering: Monthly deep soak in summer for pots; in-ground plants live on rainfall
Agave.temperature: Loves heat; hardiness varies wildly by species (-20 °C to frost-tender)

Nephrolepis.npk: Dilute balanced feed (e.g., 20-10-20 at quarter strength)
tips: Ferns have delicate roots - always err on the weak side
Pale, slow fronds in summer = time for a light feed
Nephrolepis.watering: Keep evenly moist always — a dry Boston fern sheds leaflets like confetti
Nephrolepis.humidity: High (60%+); the classic humid-porch and bathroom fern

Pinus.npk: Rarely needed; acid evergreen feed (e.g., 4-3-4 with sulfur) if weak
Pinus.fertilizer: Holly-tone type acid fertilizer, or just pine needle mulch
Pinus.schedule: Early spring, only for young or clearly struggling trees
tips: Established pines in the landscape almost never need fertilizer
Let fallen needles stay - they are the tree feeding itself
Pinus.watering: Only young trees: deeply every 1-2 weeks their first two summers
Pinus.temperature: Hardy across a huge range; established pines ignore weather
Pinus.humidity: Low to average; needs free-draining soil

Juniperus.npk: Light evergreen feed (e.g., 16-4-8 slow release) if color is poor
Juniperus.schedule: Early spring at most; established plants usually need none
tips: Junipers tolerate poor soil by design
Yellowing is more often spider mites or wet feet than hunger
Juniperus.watering: Established junipers rarely need any; new plants deeply weekly for a season
Juniperus.humidity: Low; humid shade is the one thing junipers hate

Thuja.schedule: Early spring; a hedge being pushed for growth can get a second feed in late spring
tips: Feed hedges you're still growing; mature screens need little
Water deeply after feeding - thujas are shallow-rooted
Thuja.watering: Weekly deep soak for hedges in dry spells — shallow roots brown quickly in drought
Thuja.temperature: Cold-hardy; browning in winter wind is common and usually recovers
Thuja.humidity: Moderate; mulch the shallow root zone

Cactaceae.npk: Low nitrogen, higher P-K (e.g., 2-7-7), well diluted
Cactaceae.schedule: Monthly at half strength during spring/summer growth; none in winter rest
tips: Winter dormancy must be dry and unfed - that's what triggers flowers
Overfed cacti grow fast, soft, and out of character
Cactaceae.watering: Every 2-4 weeks in summer (soak and dry); near-zero in winter rest
Cactaceae.temperature: Warm summers; most want a cool (8-13 °C) dry winter to trigger flowering

Orchidaceae.schedule: Quarter strength weekly while growing; flush with plain water monthly
tips: Orchid roots in bark get almost no nutrients naturally - but burn easily
Ease off while blooming
Orchidaceae.watering: Soak and drain when the medium approaches dry — roughly weekly; never soggy bark
Orchidaceae.temperature: Most: 18-29 °C days; cooler nights encourage blooming

Crassulaceae.npk: Low nitrogen cactus feed (e.g., 2-7-7) at half strength
tips: Succulents prefer lean living - overfeeding causes stretching and rot
Never feed dormant or freshly repotted plants
Crassulaceae.watering: Soak fully, then dry fully — every 2-3 weeks in growth, barely in winter

Poaceae.npk: Lawn: nitrogen-forward (e.g., 20-5-10). Ornamental grasses: little to none
Poaceae.fertilizer: Slow-release lawn fertilizer; compost for ornamentals
Poaceae.schedule: Lawns: late spring and early fall. Ornamental grasses: once in spring at most
tips: Fall feeding builds roots; spring feeding builds mowing work
Ornamental grasses flop when overfed
Poaceae.watering: Lawns: 2-3 cm per week in one or two deep sessions; ornamental grasses: rarely once established
Poaceae.humidity: Deep infrequent watering grows deep roots; nightly sprinkles grow fungus

tips: The whole family demands acidic soil - pH first, fertilizer second
Fine shallow roots: underfeed, and mulch with pine bark
Ericaceae.watering: Shallow roots want constant light moisture — weekly deep watering plus mulch
Ericaceae.humidity: Moderate to high; hot dry wind scorches them

Arecaceae.npk: Palm formula with magnesium and manganese (e.g., 8-2-12 + Mg)
Arecaceae.fertilizer: Dedicated palm fertilizer - palms have unique micronutrient needs
Arecaceae.schedule: Every 2-3 months in the growing season
tips: Yellow banding on fronds = magnesium deficiency, classic in palms
Never cut green fronds - palms pull nutrients back from old leaves
Arecaceae.watering: When the top 3-5 cm dries — weekly indoors; more for outdoor palms in sand
Arecaceae.humidity: Moderate to high; brown tips track dry air

Lamiaceae.npk: Light balanced feed; most prefer lean soil
Lamiaceae.fertilizer: Compost; dilute liquid feed for potted herbs
tips: Overfeeding herbs trades flavor for bulk
Harvest often - it's better than fertilizer for bushy growth
Lamiaceae.watering: Most (Mediterranean types) want drying between waterings; mint is the wet exception
Lamiaceae.humidity: Low to moderate; airflow keeps leaves healthy

Rosaceae.npk: Balanced feed, low nitrogen for fruiting types (e.g., 5-10-10)
Rosaceae.fertilizer: Granular balanced or fruit tree fertilizer
Rosaceae.schedule: Early spring; fruiting types again after fruit set
tips: Watch for fire blight in this family - avoid overfeeding nitrogen
Judge trees by annual shoot growth before feeding
Rosaceae.watering: Deeply weekly for young plants and during fruit development
Rosaceae.temperature: Mostly hardy; bloom time frost is the danger window
Rosaceae.humidity: Average, with pruning for airflow — this family catches every fungus going

Fabaceae.npk: Low nitrogen (they fix their own), modest P-K
tips: Nitrogen-fixing roots mean most legumes feed themselves
Phosphorus helps nodulation and flowering
Fabaceae.watering: 2-3 cm per week, most important at flowering and pod set
Fabaceae.humidity: Moderate; wet foliage spreads bean diseases — water the base

Asteraceae.npk: Light balanced feed (e.g., 5-5-5); most bloom better lean
Asteraceae.fertilizer: Compost at planting plus occasional liquid feed
tips: Most daisies overfed = tall, floppy, flower-shy
Deadhead for more blooms instead of feeding more
Asteraceae.watering: Weekly deep watering; most get tough once established
Asteraceae.humidity: Low to moderate; crowded damp beds invite mildew

Cucurbitaceae.npk: Balanced early, high potassium at fruiting
Cucurbitaceae.schedule: At planting, at flowering, and monthly while fruiting
tips: Heavy feeders - plant into compost mounds
Steady water prevents bitter fruit
Cucurbitaceae.watering: Heavy: 2-5 cm per week at the base, daily in heat waves

Solanaceae.npk: Balanced early, low-N high-K at flowering (tomato food)
Solanaceae.schedule: At transplant, then every 2 weeks from first flowers
tips: Even watering prevents blossom end rot
Go easy on nitrogen once flowering starts
Solanaceae.watering: Deep and even — 2-3× a week; fluctuation causes cracked fruit and blossom end rot
Solanaceae.humidity: Moderate; always water at the base

Amaryllidaceae.schedule: At planting and as foliage emerges
tips: Feed the foliage phase - that builds next year's bulb
Let leaves die back naturally
Amaryllidaceae.watering: Moist during leaf growth, tapering to dry dormancy
Amaryllidaceae.temperature: Hardy bulbs need winter chill; tender ones (amaryllis) 18-24 °C

Pinaceae.npk: Rarely needed; acid evergreen feed if young or weak
Pinaceae.fertilizer: Acid-formula evergreen fertilizer or needle mulch
tips: Established conifers rarely benefit from fertilizer
Browning is usually water, salt, or pests - not hunger
Pinaceae.watering: Young conifers deeply every 1-2 weeks; established ones only in extreme drought

default.npk: Balanced fertilizer (e.g., 10-10-10) at half the label strength
default.fertilizer: All-purpose balanced feed: granular slow-release outdoors, liquid for pots
default.schedule: Spring and early summer for garden plants; monthly in the growing season (never winter) for houseplants
tips: When unsure, underfeed: almost every plant recovers from hunger faster than from fertilizer burn
Feed only during active growth, onto moist (not dry) soil
Yellow older leaves often mean nitrogen hunger; scorched leaf edges often mean overfeeding
default.watering: Water deeply when the top 2-3 cm of soil feels dry; most plants prefer deep-and-infrequent over little-and-often
default.temperature: Most garden and house plants are comfortable at 18-24 °C; protect from frost unless known hardy
default.humidity: Average humidity suits most plants; keep soil moist but never waterlogged, with drainage holes always
